summary: The Pulmonary vascular resistance calculator turns the left Arterial Pressure, the cardiac Output and the pulmonary Vascular Resistance into mean Pulmonary Arterial Pressure (MPAP). It is built for an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Pulmonary vascular resistance calculator work?
sections.html:
The Pulmonary vascular resistance calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports mean Pulmonary Arterial Pressure (MPAP) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the left Arterial Pressure (LAP), the cardiac Output (CO) and the pulmonary Vascular Resistance (PVR).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • A number, expressed in L/min.
  • A number, expressed in dynes · sec · cm-5.

sections.title: The formula behind the Pulmonary vascular resistance calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Mean Pulmonary Arterial Pressure (MPAP)=(1 ÷ 80) × cardiac Output (CO) × pulmonary Vascular Resistance (PVR) + left Arterial Pressure (LAP)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Left Arterial Pressure (LAP) = 10 mmHg, Cardiac Output (CO) = 10 and Pulmonary Vascular Resistance (PVR) = 10. Working through the relationship above gives Mean Pulmonary Arterial Pressure (MPAP) = 10.0013 mmHg.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Mean Pulmonary Arterial Pressure (MPAP) = 10.0013 mmHg should be roughly the size you expected from Left Arterial Pressure (LAP) = 10 mmHg and Cardiac Output (CO) = 10.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in millimeters of mercury, and convertible to any of the 28 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Pressure, opening in millimeters of mercury
  • Pressure, opening in millimeters of mercury

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Pulmonary vascular resistance calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the left Arterial Pressure, the cardiac Output and the pulmonary Vascular Resistance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Pulmonary vascular resistance calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

faq.q: What does the Pulmonary vascular resistance calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns mean Pulmonary Arterial Pressure (MPAP), derived from the left Arterial Pressure, the cardiac Output and the pulmonary Vascular Resistance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Pulmonary vascular resistance calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the left Arterial Pressure, the cardiac Output and the pulmonary Vascular Resistance, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter mean Pulmonary Arterial Pressure (MPAP) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Mean Pulmonary Arterial Pressure (MPAP) opens in millimeters of mercury and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Mean Pulmonary Arterial Pressure (MPAP) = 10.0013 mmHg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Pulmonary vascular resistance calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
